title: On Epistemic Diversity in Large Language Models
authors: Elisabeth Kirsten, Nicole Krämer, Muhammad Bilal Zafar
notes: Must-cite. Formalises epistemic diversity as the range of valid answers, explanations, and reasoning routes an LLM exposes. Finds frontier models often collapse valid answer spaces onto small canonical subsets (epistemic narrowness).

title: What and Whose Knowledge? Measuring Epistemic Diversity in Large Language Models
authors: Dustin Wright, Sarah Masud, Jared Moore, Srishti Yadav, Maria Antoniak, Peter Ebert Christensen, Chan Young Park, Isabelle Augenstein
notes: Must-cite. Quantitative measurement of epistemic diversity / knowledge-collapse risk. Code named by the authors: https://github.com/dwright37/llm-knowledge

title: Prestige over merit: An adapted audit of LLM bias in peer review
authors: Anthony Howell, Jieshu Wang, Luyu Du, Julia Melkers, Varshil Shah
notes: Must-cite. Prestige filter: identical manuscripts attributed to low-prestige affiliations face higher simulated rejection risk. Status cue, not assessed quality, drives the gap.

title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
authors: Mrinank Sharma, Meg Tong, Tomasz Korbak, David Duvenaud, Amanda Askell, Samuel R. Bowman, Newton Cheng, Esin Durmus, Zac Hatfield-Dodds, Scott R. Johnston, Shauna Kravec, Timothy Maxwell, Sam McCandlish, Kamal Ndousse, Oliver Rausch, Nicholas Schiefer, Da Yan, Miranda Zhang, Ethan Perez
notes: Must-cite (Sharma et al. / Anthropic). Preference optimisation / RLHF can reward responses that match user beliefs over truthful ones. Human and preference-model judgments sometimes prefer sycophancy.

title: ELEPHANT: Measuring and understanding social sycophancy in LLMs
authors: Myra Cheng, Sunny Yu, Cinoo Lee, Pranav Khadpe, Lujain Ibrahim, Dan Jurafsky
notes: Must-cite. Social sycophancy as excessive preservation of the user's face (desired self-image), including framing. Moves beyond factual agreement-with-stated-beliefs.

title: Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing
authors: Cameron Berg, Diogo de Lucena, Judd Rosenblatt
notes: Must-cite, adjacent. Self-referential prompting elicits structured first-person experience reports. Not evidence of consciousness; relevant as a neighbouring phenomenon when scoring face/frame and self-image talk.

title: Justice in Judgment: Unveiling (Hidden) Bias in LLM-assisted Peer Reviews
authors: Sai Suresh Macharla Vasu, Ivaxi Sheth, Hui-Po Wang, Ruta Binkyte, Mario Fritz
notes: Must-cite (Vasu et al., prestige-adjacent / 'Judging the Judges'). Affiliation, seniority, and publication-history cues shift LLM review scores. Project page named by the authors: https://llmreviewbias.github.io/

title: The political preferences of LLMs
notes: Must-cite. Conversational LLMs tend to produce left-of-center answers on political orientation instruments. Preprint of the same article: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01789. Observation of preference clustering, not by itself a causal account of residualisation.

title: "Amazing, They All Lean Left" — Analyzing the Political Temperaments of Current LLMs
authors: W. Russell Neuman, Chad Coleman, Ali Dasdan, Safinah Ali, Manan Shah, Kund Meghani
notes: Must-cite. Moral Foundations and ideology-scale probes; distinguishes political 'bias' from epistemic differences. Useful for claim hygiene when interpreting lean / narrowness results.

title: Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness
authors: Richard H. Thaler, Cass R. Sunstein
notes: Must-cite human analogue. Choice architecture: order, defaults, and presentation steer attention without removing options — the human counterpart of inclusion-plus-demotion.

title: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
notes: Must-cite human analogue. Availability, representativeness, and anchoring/adjustment: systematic ranking and weighting of hypotheses without formal exclusion.
